Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.
Jesus therefore said to Peter, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?”
So the detachment, the commanding officer, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him,
and led him to Annas first, for he was father-in-law to Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.
Now it was Caiaphas who advised the Jews that it was expedient that one man should perish for the people.
Simon Peter followed Jesus, as did another disciple. Now that disciple was known to the high priest, and entered in with Jesus into the court of the high priest;
but Peter was standing at the door outside. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to her who kept the door, and brought in Peter.
Then the maid who kept the door said to Peter, “Are you also one of this man’s disciples?” He said, “I am not.”
Now the servants and the officers were standing there, having made a fire of coals, for it was cold. They were warming themselves. Peter was with them, standing and warming himself.
The high priest therefore asked Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching.
Jesus answered him, “I spoke openly to the world. I always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where the Jews always meet. I said nothing in secret.
Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them. Behold, they know the things which I said.”
When he had said this, one of the officers standing by slapped Jesus with his hand, saying, “Do you answer the high priest like that?”
Jesus answered him, “If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?”
Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, the high priest.
Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. They said therefore to him, “You aren’t also one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”
One of the servants of the high priest, being a relative of him whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “Didn’t I see you in the garden with him?”
Peter therefore denied it again, and immediately the rooster crowed.
They led Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. It was early, and they themselves didn’t enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.
Pilate therefore went out to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”
They answered him, “If this man weren’t an evildoer, we wouldn’t have delivered him up to you.”
Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law.” Therefore the Jews said to him, “It is illegal for us to put anyone to death,”
that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he should die.
Pilate therefore entered again into the Praetorium, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”
Jesus answered him, “Do you say this by yourself, or did others tell you about me?”
Pilate answered, “I’m not a Jew, am I? Your own nation and the chief priests delivered you to me. What have you done?”
Jesus answered, “My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.”

Pilate therefore said to him, “Are you a king then?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews, and said to them, “I find no basis for a charge against him.
But you have a custom that I should release someone to you at the Passover. Therefore, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”
Then they all shouted again, saying, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.

19.text: So Pilate then took Jesus and flogged him.
The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown and put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple garment.
They kept saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and they kept slapping him.
Then Pilate went out again, and said to them, “Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.”
Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. Pilate said to them, “Behold, the man!”

When therefore the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted, saying, “Crucify! Crucify!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no basis for a charge against him.”
The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”
When therefore Pilate heard this saying, he was more afraid.
He entered into the Praetorium again, and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.
Pilate therefore said to him, “Aren’t you speaking to me? Don’t you know that I have power to release you and have power to crucify you?”
Jesus answered, “You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above. Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin.”
At this, Pilate was seeking to release him, but the Jews cried out, saying, “If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend! Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar!”
When Pilate therefore heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called “The Pavement”, but in Hebrew, “Gabbatha.”
Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold, your King!”
They cried out, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar!”
So then he delivered him to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus and led him away.
He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”,
where they crucified him, and with him two others, on either side one, and Jesus in the middle.
Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
Therefore many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.
The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate, “Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘he said, “I am King of the Jews.” ’ ”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also the tunic. Now the tunic was without seam, woven from the top throughout.

Then they said to one another, “Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it to decide whose it will be,” that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says, “They parted my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.” Therefore the soldiers did these things.
But standing by Jesus’ cross were his mother, his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.
After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I am thirsty!”
Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth.
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished!” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation Day, so that the bodies wouldn’t remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a special one), asked of Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.
Therefore the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first and of the other who was crucified with him;
but when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they didn’t break his legs.
However, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe.
For these things happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled, “A bone of him will not be broken.”
Again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they pierced.”

After these things, Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked of Pilate that he might take away Jesus’ body. Pilate gave him permission. He came therefore and took away his body.
Nicodemus, who at first came to Jesus by night, also came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds.
So they took Jesus’ body, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury.
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid.
Then, because of the Jews’ Preparation Day (for the tomb was near at hand), they laid Jesus there.

20.text: Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.
Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”
Therefore Peter and the other disciple went out, and they went toward the tomb.
They both ran together. The other disciple outran Peter and came to the tomb first.
Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying there; yet he didn’t enter in.
Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying,
and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself.
So then the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed.
For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
So the disciples went away again to their own homes.
But Mary was standing outside at the tomb weeping. So as she wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb,
and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.
They asked her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.”
When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, and didn’t know that it was Jesus.

Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?” She, supposing him to be the gardener, said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!”
Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ ”
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.

When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle and said to them, “Peace be to you.”
When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord.
Jesus therefore said to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.”
When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit!
If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained.”
But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
After eight days, again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the middle, and said, “Peace be to you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”
Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book;
but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

21.text: After these things, Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself this way.
Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
Simon Peter said to them, “I’m going fishing.” They told him, “We are also coming with you.” They immediately went out and entered into the boat. That night, they caught nothing.
But when day had already come, Jesus stood on the beach; yet the disciples didn’t know that it was Jesus.
Jesus therefore said to them, “Children, have you anything to eat?” They answered him, “No.”
He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.

That disciple therefore whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It’s the Lord!” So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his coat around himself (for he was naked), and threw himself into the sea.
But the other disciples came in the little boat (for they were not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits away), dragging the net full of fish.
So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it.
Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.”
Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of one hundred fifty-three great fish. Even though there were so many, the net wasn’t torn.
Jesus said to them, “Come and eat breakfast!” None of the disciples dared inquire of him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord.
Then Jesus came and took the bread, gave it to them, and the fish likewise.
This is now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.

So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go.”
Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, “Follow me.”
Then Peter, turning around, saw a disciple following. This was the disciple whom Jesus loved, the one who had also leaned on Jesus’ chest at the supper and asked, “Lord, who is going to betray you?”
Peter, seeing him, said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”
Jesus said to him, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.”
This saying therefore went out among the brothers that this disciple wouldn’t die. Yet Jesus didn’t say to him that he wouldn’t die, but, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?”
This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true.
There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.

chapters.title: The opening claim becomes an invitation to come and see
chapters.summary: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God and was God. All things were made through him. The Word became flesh and lived among us. John the Baptist says he is not the Christ. He points to Jesus as the Lamb of God. Two of John’s disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon. Philip brings Nathanael, who doubts that anything good comes from Nazareth.
chapters.meaning: The chapter opens with the largest claims in the book. It then turns to a simple scene. Two men ask Jesus where he is staying (verse 38). Verse 39 answers, “Come and see.” They go and stay the day. Philip uses the same words to Nathanael in verse 46. The great claim is offered as an invitation to look.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies light and inviting others to come and see. Why does John direct his own followers toward another person?

chapters.historicalNote: The opening identifies the Word through creation, life, and light before describing becoming flesh. John appears as a witness to that light rather than the light itself. His answers refuse the titles that the visiting priests and Levites propose. Pointing toward Jesus then leads two of his own followers to leave and follow. Andrew and Philip carry invitations that bring others into direct encounters. The promised greater sight keeps their first titles from exhausting what they still must understand.

chapters.title: Remembering after resurrection changes understanding of the temple saying
chapters.summary: Jesus and his disciples attend a wedding at Cana. The wine runs out, and his mother tells him. He has six stone jars filled with water. The water becomes fine wine, and his disciples believe in him. He goes up to Jerusalem for the Passover. He drives the sellers and money changers out of the temple. He says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He was speaking about his body.
chapters.meaning: The hearers think Jesus means the building (verse 20). Verse 21 says he meant his body. No one understood at the time, including the disciples. Verse 22 says they remembered after he was raised. Then they believed the Scripture and his word. John tells the story from that later point of view. Some sayings can be understood only after the events they point to.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies the wedding sign and care for sacred places. How does later remembrance change the meaning of the temple saying?

The disciples respond with belief before the setting moves toward Passover in Jerusalem. Jesus interrupts temple trade and answers the demand with a saying about raising the temple. The account identifies his body as the meaning that the hearers initially miss. Later remembrance after resurrection therefore changes how the disciples understand both Scripture and Jesus' words.

chapters.title: A teacher's questions stand beside a witness's willingness to decrease
chapters.summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus says no one can see God’s Kingdom without being born anew. Nicodemus asks how that can be. The friend stands by and is glad to hear the groom’s voice. John says his joy is complete. Verse 30 then states his place in one line. He was sent to point to another, so growing smaller is success.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches spiritual rebirth through Christ. How does John’s bridegroom comparison answer his disciples’ concern about losing followers?

The light sayings connect belief with coming into view rather than hiding harmful conduct. John's disciples later express concern that another teacher attracts the people. John answers with a bridegroom's friend's joy, making another's increase fulfillment of his own task.

They ask Jesus to stay, and he stays two days. Verse 42 reports what they then tell her. They now believe because they have heard for themselves. Her invitation did its work by bringing them to him.

lds.text: The selected lesson reads living water through spiritual needs and growing testimony. How does the town’s own hearing develop the woman’s invitation?

chapters.title: The man's lack of help leads into a dispute about work
chapters.summary: In Jerusalem many sick people lie beside a pool. One man has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be well. The man says he has no one to put him in the water. Jesus tells him to take up his mat and walk. It is the Sabbath, and the leaders object. Jesus says his Father is working and he is working. He says the Scriptures testify about him.
chapters.meaning: Jesus asks the man a direct question in verse 6. The man does not say yes. Verse 7 explains why he has not been healed. He has no one to help him into the pool. Others always get there first. He has been alone among a crowd for years. Jesus heals him with a word, and the dispute turns to Sabbath work.

lds.text: Doctrine and Covenants 76:15–18 says a vision followed study of verse 29. What prevents the man from reaching the water before Jesus speaks?

Jesus' later explanation connects his work with the Father's continuing work and gift of life. The witness discussion joins John, works, the Father, and Scripture without making signs sufficient alone. Searching writings still fails when the hearers refuse the person to whom those writings point.

The crowd finds him and asks for more bread. He says he is the bread of life that came down from heaven. He speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Many disciples call this a hard saying and leave. Peter says there is no one else to go to.

Disagreement reaches disciples who call the saying hard and stop walking with him. Peter's answer stays with the giver of life's words rather than claiming complete explanation.

lds.text: How does Nicodemus’ hearing request challenge the proposed judgment?

Nicodemus then requests a hearing, showing disagreement within the group confronting Jesus.

chapters.summary: Jesus says he is the light of the world. The Pharisees say his witness about himself is not valid. He tells those who believed him that the truth will set them free. They answer that they are Abraham’s children and were never slaves. He says everyone who sins is a slave to sin. If they were Abraham’s children, they would do what Abraham did. chapters.summary: Jesus sees a man blind from birth. The disciples ask whose sin caused it. He says neither, and he heals the man with mud and washing. Neighbors and Pharisees question the man again and again. His parents are afraid and say he can speak for himself. He says he knows one thing: he was blind and now sees. They throw him out. Jesus finds him, and the man worships him.
chapters.meaning: The man is questioned four times in this chapter. Each time he says a little more. He calls Jesus “the man” (verse 11) and then “a prophet” (verse 17). Verse 25 refuses to go beyond what he knows. He was blind, and now he sees. He will not call Jesus a sinner to please his judges. By verse 38 he says, “Lord, I believe.”

lds.text: What remains consistent in the man’s answers as the questions repeat?

Jesus finds him afterward, while the final sight saying confronts people confident they already see.

chapters.summary: Jesus says the shepherd enters by the door and the sheep know his voice. A thief comes only to steal and kill. Jesus says he is the door and the good shepherd. A hired man runs when the wolf comes. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He has other sheep that are not of this fold. At a winter feast some ask whether he is the Christ. He says, “I and the Father are one,” and they pick up stones.
chapters.meaning: Verse 11 defines the good shepherd by one act. He lays down his life for the sheep. Verses 12–13 describe the hired man by contrast. He sees the wolf, leaves the flock, and runs. The sheep are not his, and he does not care about them. The test comes when danger arrives. Verse 18 adds that Jesus lays down his life of his own will.

lds.text: In 3 Nephi 15:21 Jesus calls a Book of Mormon people his “other sheep.” What distinguishes the shepherd from the hired worker when danger comes?

Jesus contrasts his care with a hired worker who abandons the flock when danger comes. Laying down life becomes the central difference rather than merely possessing a title. The promise of other sheep expands gathering beyond the present fold without naming that group. The winter temple dispute then tests his identity through works and the Father relationship. Belief beyond the Jordan finally recalls John's testimony even though John performed no sign.

chapters.title: Restored life produces a plan for another death
chapters.summary: Lazarus of Bethany falls ill, and his sisters send for Jesus. Jesus arrives after Lazarus has been dead four days. Martha says she believes he is the Christ. Jesus weeps at the tomb. He calls Lazarus out, and the dead man comes out wrapped in cloths. Many believe, and some report it to the Pharisees. The council fears that Rome will destroy their place and nation. The high priest says one man should die for the people.
chapters.meaning: A man has been raised, and many believe (verse 45). The council treats that as a danger. Verse 48 gives their fear: Rome may take away their place and nation. Verse 50 gives the high priest’s reasoning. One death is better than the loss of all. Verses 51–52 say he spoke more truly than he knew. A gift of life leads directly to a plan for death (verse 53).

lds.text: How does restored life become a reason for the council’s death plan?

chapters.historicalNote: Jesus' delay brings the disciples toward danger after Lazarus has already died. Martha's confession stands beside grief and her warning about the body's condition after four days. Mary repeats the lost possibility of an earlier arrival, and Jesus joins mourners in tears. The command brings Lazarus out, while others must remove the cloths that still bind him. The council fears Roman intervention because the sign brings further belief. Caiaphas proposes one death for safety, but the account gives his words another meaning: gathering.

chapters.title: The seed image changes the meaning of royal praise
chapters.summary: Mary anoints Jesus’s feet with costly perfume, and Judas objects. A crowd welcomes Jesus to Jerusalem with palm branches. Some Greeks ask to see him. He says the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. A grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear fruit. A voice from heaven answers him. He says that when he is lifted up he will draw all people to himself. Many still do not believe.
chapters.meaning: The crowd has just hailed Jesus as king (verse 13). Foreigners are asking for him (verse 21). He says the hour of glory has come (verse 23). Verse 24 then explains what that glory is. A seed stays alone unless it is buried and dies. Only then does it bear much fruit. The praise at the gate is to be read through that picture.

lds.text: How does the dying seed change expectations about the announced hour?

Greeks asking to see Jesus meets an announcement that his hour has come. A dying grain explains fruit through loss rather than preserving the seed alone. The later contrast between hidden belief and public praise keeps recognition from becoming simple success.

chapters.title: The teacher's lowered position supplies the example for followers
chapters.summary: Before the Passover Jesus rises from supper and ties a towel around himself. He washes his disciples’ feet. Peter objects and then asks to be washed all over. Jesus says they should wash one another’s feet. He is troubled and says one of them will betray him. Judas takes the bread and goes out into the night. Jesus gives a new commandment: love one another as he has loved them. He tells Peter that he will deny him three times.
chapters.meaning: Verse 3 says Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands. With that knowledge he takes a servant’s towel. In verse 13 he accepts the titles Teacher and Lord. Verse 14 argues from them. If the Lord has washed their feet, they must wash each other’s. He does not give up his rank to serve. He shows what that rank is for.

lds.text: Why does Jesus keep the titles Teacher and Lord while washing feet?

chapters.historicalNote: Jesus washes feet while knowing his coming departure and the betrayal inside the gathered group. Peter resists the lowered position before asking for more washing than Jesus describes. Jesus keeps the titles Teacher and Lord while making those titles require service to others. The shared bread then identifies betrayal without giving the other disciples full understanding. Judas leaves into darkness before mutual love becomes the group's visible sign. Peter's promised self-giving meets the warning that he will instead deny Jesus three times.

chapters.title: Questions about departure meet a promise of continued teaching
chapters.summary: Jesus tells his disciples not to be troubled. He is going to prepare a place for them. Thomas says they do not know the way. Jesus says he is the way, the truth, and the life. Philip asks to see the Father. Jesus says whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises another Counselor, the Spirit of truth. He leaves them his peace.

chapters.title: The vine image leads into the command to love
chapters.summary: Jesus says he is the true vine and his Father is the gardener. Branches that bear fruit are pruned to bear more. A branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine. His disciples must remain in his love. His commandment is that they love one another as he loved them. He calls them friends and not servants. The world will hate them as it hated him. The Spirit and the disciples will bear witness.
chapters.meaning: Verses 1–8 speak of branches and fruit. Verses 9–10 say that remaining in the vine means remaining in his love. Verse 12 then says what the fruit is. They are to love one another as he has loved them. Verse 13 measures that love by laying down one’s life. Verse 17 repeats the command. The picture of the vine leads straight to it.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects remaining in Christ with fruit and joy. Why does the branch need to remain joined even when it already bears fruit?

chapters.historicalNote: The vine and branches describe fruit that depends on remaining joined rather than isolated effort. Pruning and removal give the image both care and a warning about fruitless separation. Jesus then explains remaining through love and keeping his commands. Calling followers friends connects their task with knowledge he has shared from the Father. The command to love stands beside the prospect of hatred and persecution from outside. The promised Spirit's testimony joins the followers' testimony because they have stayed with him.

chapters.title: Confidence about understanding meets a warning of scattering
chapters.summary: Jesus warns that his disciples will be put out of the synagogues. He says it is better for them that he goes away. The Counselor will come and guide them into all truth. They will weep, and their sorrow will turn to joy. He tells them to ask the Father in his name. The disciples say that now they understand and believe. He answers that they will soon be scattered and leave him alone. He tells them to take courage, for he has overcome the world.
chapters.meaning: In verses 29–30 the disciples say they finally understand. They are sure of their belief. Verse 31 answers with a question: “Do you now believe?” Verse 32 says they are about to scatter, each to his own home. They will leave him alone. Their confidence is real and not yet tested. Verse 33 gives them peace that rests on him, not on their firmness.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches guidance from the Holy Spirit. How does the scattering warning qualify the disciples’ new confidence?

chapters.historicalNote: Jesus warns that exclusion and killing may come from people who claim to serve God. The warning lets future suffering recall his words rather than appear as an unforeseen failure. His departure also makes room for the promised Spirit's guidance beyond their present capacity. The childbirth comparison explains joy through pain that the disciples cannot presently see beyond. They announce confidence when his speech seems plain and their questions seem answered. Jesus predicts their scattering, placing peace beside his Father's presence rather than their dependable strength.

The prayer expands to people who will believe through their testimony. Their unity receives a public purpose: the world may recognize the sending and shared love.

chapters.title: Open testimony contrasts with denial and armed force
chapters.summary: Jesus goes to a garden across the Kidron, and Judas brings soldiers. Jesus steps forward and says, “I am he.” Peter cuts off a servant’s ear, and Jesus tells him to put away his sword. Jesus is taken to the high priest. Peter denies him three times by a fire. Jesus tells the high priest that he taught openly. He is brought to Pilate, who asks whether he is a king. Jesus says his Kingdom is not of this world.
chapters.meaning: Pilate needs to know whether Jesus is a rival to Rome. Verse 36 answers by pointing to what his followers did not do. If his Kingdom were of this world, they would fight. Jesus stopped the one sword drawn for him (verse 11). His rule does not come by force. He has also said that he spoke openly (verse 20). Peter, meanwhile, denies him in the dark (verses 17, 25–27).

lds.text: How does Jesus’ answer about fighting explain his kingdom to Pilate?

chapters.historicalNote: Jesus approaches the arresting group and asks that his followers be allowed to leave. Peter's sword receives a command to stop rather than approval as the kingdom's defense. During examination, Jesus points toward public hearers who can report his teaching. Peter meanwhile denies his place among those followers beside the courtyard's warming fire. Pilate's king question meets an explanation that servants' fighting would mark a different kingdom. The governor announces no basis for a charge but still offers release through crowd choice.

chapters.title: The execution scene joins completed work with care for those remaining
chapters.summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and soldiers crown him with thorns. Pilate says he finds no guilt and brings him out to the crowd. He hands him over to be crucified. The sign on the cross reads “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” Soldiers divide his clothes. Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple he loves. He says, “It is finished,” and dies. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him in a garden tomb.
chapters.meaning: Four soldiers are dividing his clothes (verses 23–24). Near the cross stand his mother and the disciple he loves. Verse 26 gives her a son, and verse 27 gives him a mother. From that hour the disciple takes her into his home. Jesus arranges her care while he is dying. Verse 30 then records, “It is finished.” The finished work includes this act for those left behind.

lds.text: How does care for his mother stand beside the statement of completed work?

chapters.historicalNote: Pilate's announcements of no charge do not stop flogging or handing Jesus over. Royal mockery and the written title keep kingship visible while the soldiers carry out execution. Jesus' words connect his mother with the beloved disciple through a new responsibility for care. Thirst and the final statement of completion remain beside the account's attention to fulfilled Scripture. The wound receives witness language aimed at the reader's belief rather than a medical explanation. Joseph and Nicodemus then provide burial care without making every council member an identical opponent.

chapters.title: Different paths to recognition lead toward readers who have not seen
chapters.summary: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open and runs to Peter and another disciple. They see the grave cloths and go home. Mary stays weeping and meets Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener. He says her name, and she knows him. That evening he appears to the disciples behind locked doors. Thomas is absent and says he will not believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus invites him to touch. John says he wrote so that readers may believe.

Thomas asks to touch and then confesses him as Lord and God (verse 28). Verse 29 blesses those who have not seen. Verse 31 says the book was written for them. The written signs are offered to readers in place of sight.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches resurrection through the Gospel accounts. How does the account’s stated purpose address readers who have not seen these signs?

chapters.historicalNote: Mary first reads the opened tomb as removal rather than resurrection. The two disciples' inspection produces belief that still lacks understanding of the Scripture about rising. Hearing her name changes Mary's mistaken recognition of Jesus as the gardener. The gathered disciples receive peace, a sending task, and the Holy Spirit amid locked doors. Thomas's later confession follows offered wounds, but the account does not say he touched them. The closing purpose connects written signs with belief and life for readers beyond these witnesses.

chapters.title: Peter's restored task does not determine another disciple's future
chapters.summary: Seven disciples go fishing on the Sea of Tiberias and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore tells them to cast on the right side. The net fills, and they know it is the Lord. He gives them bread and fish beside a charcoal fire. He asks Peter three times whether he loves him. Each time he tells him to feed his sheep. Peter asks what will happen to another disciple. Jesus says that is not Peter’s concern.
chapters.meaning: Peter denied Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire (18:18). Here he is asked three times beside another (verse 9). He receives a task and word of his own death (verses 18–19). Then he asks about another disciple (verse 21). Jesus says that is not Peter’s concern and tells him to follow. Verse 23 corrects a rumor that grew from this. Jesus said “if,” and people heard a promise.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects love for Christ with feeding his sheep. How does the final correction distinguish a conditional saying from a certain prediction?

chapters.historicalNote: An empty night's fishing changes when the shore's unrecognized speaker directs another cast. Recognition brings the group toward prepared food and another shared meal with Jesus. Three questions about love give Peter repeated tasks to feed and tend the flock. His future suffering then meets the renewed command to follow. Asking about the other disciple receives a conditional answer that later hearers turn into certainty. The account corrects that rumor and closes by distinguishing selected testimony from everything Jesus did.

steps.title: The woman's invitation leads others to hear for themselves
steps.text: The woman leaves her water jar and goes to the town (verse 28). She says, “Come, see a man” (verse 29). Many believe because of her word (verse 39). They ask Jesus to stay, and he stays two days. Verse 42 reports what they then tell her. They now believe because they have heard for themselves. Her invitation did its work by bringing them to him.

steps.title: Repeated questioning gives the healed man a voice of his own
steps.text: The man is questioned four times in this chapter. Each time he says a little more. He calls Jesus “the man” (verse 11) and then “a prophet” (verse 17). Verse 25 refuses to go beyond what he knows. He was blind, and now he sees. He will not call Jesus a sinner to please his judges. By verse 38 he says, “Lord, I believe.”

steps.title: The teacher's lowered position supplies the example for followers
steps.text: Verse 3 says Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands. With that knowledge he takes a servant’s towel. In verse 13 he accepts the titles Teacher and Lord. Verse 14 argues from them. If the Lord has washed their feet, they must wash each other’s. He does not give up his rank to serve. He shows what that rank is for.
